analysis.one_liner: Creates a national 10-cent bottle deposit that drink makers must fund and run.
analysis.headline: A bill to require a nationwide 10-cent beverage-container deposit and make drink makers run the recycling system died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first national bottle-deposit system. Drink makers and importers would have had to set up and pay for systems to collect, transport, and recycle every bottle and can they sell, stores would charge customers a deposit of at least 10 cents per container refunded on return, and brands that fell short of an 80% return rate would have to hand their unclaimed deposits to the states. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in November 2003 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who return containers get their deposit back and gain convenient return sites; taxpayers and local waste authorities benefit because producers, rather than municipal budgets, would pay for collecting and processing the tens of billions of containers thrown away each year; the recycling industry gains a huge new stream of material, since redeemed containers could not be landfilled or incinerated. The bill's findings cite savings of roughly 300 million barrels of oil over a decade, more than 4 million tons of greenhouse gases avoided annually, and roadside beverage-container litter cut by up to 84%.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, taxpayers, and local recycling programs

how_it_helps.text: Shifts the cost of dealing with used beverage containers from local waste authorities and taxpayers to the drink makers who put the containers into commerce, requiring each brand owner to run an effective redemption, transport, processing, and reporting system.

Gives every consumer a cash incentive to recycle: sellers collect a deposit of no more than the refund value at purchase, and return sites must pay back at least 10 cents per container — an amount adjusted upward with inflation every 10 years — in cash or a voucher redeemable on demand.

Sets a hard performance target: brands must achieve an 80% redemption rate, and any brand that falls short while otherwise complying must pay each state the difference between deposits collected and refunds paid, so missed recycling goals cost the industry money rather than the public.
Bars brand owners from landfilling or incinerating redeemed containers and requires independent audits of recovery rates and of deposit finances, with results made public.

The bill's own findings state that reaching 80% recycling would save the equivalent of about 300 million barrels of oil over a decade, cut greenhouse gas emissions by more than 4 million tons a year, and reduce roadside beverage-container litter by as much as 84% in states without bottle laws.
Lets states keep stronger rules of their own: nothing in the bill stops a state or locality from imposing requirements not inconsistent with it.

analysis.who_pays: Beverage brand owners — manufacturers and importers — bear the main cost: they must build and fund the collection and recycling systems, submit EPA-approved management plans with fees, and forfeit unclaimed deposits to states if redemption falls below 80%. Retailers and other sellers must collect deposits and handle returns, and consumers front the deposit at purchase, recovering it only when they return the container. Civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation (up to $10,000 for reporting violations) back the rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Beverage makers, retailers, and unreturned deposits

drawbacks.text: Consumers pay the deposit up front on every covered beverage — at least 10 cents per container — and only recover it by returning the container, so people who never bother to redeem effectively pay more for their drinks.
Retailers and return sites take on new operational burdens: collecting deposits, accepting and sorting returned containers, and resolving disputes with brand owners through binding arbitration.
New and small beverage sellers face a barrier to market: they cannot sell in interstate commerce until the EPA approves their management plan, which adds paperwork and delay for startups.

The enforcement design has a soft spot: if a brand hits the 80% redemption rate, it keeps up to a fifth of the deposits as unclaimed money, and the penalty for missing the target only kicks in for otherwise-compliant brands, giving producers room to argue over what counts as compliance.
Dairy products are excluded from the deposit requirement, so milk containers continue to be handled outside the system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but mostly refundable or borne by the industry the bill targets: consumers get their deposit back when they recycle, and the heaviest burden — financing collection and processing of tens of billions of containers a year — moves from taxpayers and municipal budgets to drink makers, which is the bill's stated purpose. The main design weakness is that unclaimed deposits stay with brand owners as long as they hit the 80% target, and the plan-approval process could slow small entrants. On balance, the findings' energy, emissions, and litter numbers are large relative to a 10-cent refundable deposit, making this a low-cost, high-benefit structure for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the two-year Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Jeffords of Vermont introduced the National Beverage Producer Responsibility Act on November 14, 2003, joined by four Democratic senators — Leahy of Vermont, Kerry of Massachusetts, Lieberman of Connecticut, and Akaka of Hawaii — with five Democratic cosponsors in all.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The action history ends there: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind for the remaining fourteen months of the 108th Congress.
The bill died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2005, without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beverage manufacturers and importers came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, they avoided a nationwide deposit-and-recycling obligation and continued to shift the cost of handling tens of billions of discarded containers each year onto local waste authorities and taxpayers.

for.name: James Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: James Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; the action history shows no activity beyond the referral.

against.name: Beverage and container industry
against.role: Soft drink, beer, and bottled-water manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Longstanding, well-documented opponent of national deposit legislation, which would make producers fund container recovery; the bill would impose exactly that obligation on brand owners.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill was introduced by an Independent senator with five Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, and it never advanced past committee referral.

industries.industry: Beverage manufacturers and importers (soft drink, beer, and bottled-water brands)
industries.note: The bill makes brand owners finance and operate the recovery of every container they sell, with EPA-approved plans, audited reports, and forfeited deposits if they miss an 80% redemption rate. Today the cost of handling those containers falls on local waste authorities and taxpayers, so blocking the bill preserved that transfer of costs to the public.

industries.industry: Grocery, convenience, and other beverage retailers
industries.note: Sellers must collect deposits at every sale, indicate them on receipts, and operate or host return sites, with disputes settled by binding arbitration. The burden is administrative, but its purpose — a working redemption network for customers — runs with the public's interest.

A national deposit stream feeding roughly 120 billion previously unrecycled containers a year into recovery, with a ban on landfilling or incinerating redeemed containers, would sharply expand material available to processors. More recycling capacity and less waste disposal is the outcome the public gets too.
